original_quotes.quote: The preceding analyses highlight the importance of adapting anonymisation strategies to the requirements of different clinical tasks. CASA achieves this through iterative evaluation and refinement of anonymisation strategies against task-specific privacy–utility requirements. To improve the efficiency of this iterative process, CASA incorporates a recursive self-improvement mechanism that leverages experience accumulation across tasks. Specifically, resulting experience is retained in two levels of memory for subsequent planning: fine-grained memory stores anonymisation configurations and evaluation results from previous runs, and coarse-grained memory summarises task-level lessons and recurring patterns. These memories guide subsequent strategy planning, reducing the need for repeated evaluations.

To quantify the contribution of accumulated experience, we compared CASA with and without memory under the same task-specific requirements. In the memory-enabled condition, CASA could retrieve experience from other tasks, whereas the memory-free condition had no access to previous cross-task experience. Both conditions retained within-task feedback-guided adaptation. Success required satisfying all privacy and utility thresholds specified for each run. As shown in Fig. 4 , with memory, the proportion of runs succeeding on the first evaluation increased from 46.4% to 62.9%, and the proportion succeeding within two evaluations increased from 57.1% to 81.4%. The mean number of strategy evaluations needed to reach a satisfactory configuration decreased by 31.3%, dropping from 2.27 to 1.56 steps. These results show that accumulated cross-task experience reduces the number of anonymisation and evaluation cycles needed for task adaptation, thus enabling CASA to identify satisfactory anonymisation strategies more efficiently.

original_quotes.quote: We formulate adaptive fast charging as a sequential decision-making problem in which a large language model (LLM) acts as the high-level policy of an intelligent battery-control agent in Fig 2 . In the first stage, supervised fine-tuning teaches the LLM the structured battery-action protocol and initializes it with conservative expert charging behavior. original_quotes.quote: 3.1 Problem Setup and Overview As shown in Figure 2 , RoboCoEvo formulates the co-evolution of an agent and a policy as an iterative process. The base policy π 0 \pi_{0} is a robotic foundation model trained on reference demonstrations 𝒟 0 \mathcal{D}_{0} . In round i i , Policy-Guided Agent Evolution (Section 3.2 ) collects rollouts of the current policy π i \pi_{i} in a set of scenarios 𝒮 \mathcal{S} . An MLLM-based agent groups the recurring failures into failure modes (FMs) and writes or revises a detector d m d_{m} and a recovery program ρ m \rho_{m} for each FM. Agent-Guided Policy Capability Expansion (Section 3.3 ) then applies these programs to the detected failure states and to perturbed copies of them, which yields the corrective experience R i = f ⁡ ( π i , 𝒮 ) . R_{i}=f(\pi_{i},\mathcal{S}). The policy is then post-trained on 𝒟 0 \mathcal{D}_{0} and the corrective experience accumulated up to round i i to obtain π i + 1 \pi_{i+1} , whose rollouts are used in the next round. RoboCoEvo observes the scene primarily through a scene state s t = ( q t , { p t k } k ∈ 𝒪 , ℱ t , I t ) s_{t}=(q_{t},\{p^{k}_{t}\}_{k\in\mathcal{O}},\mathcal{F}_{t},I_{t}) , where I t I_{t} denotes the camera images. Here, q t q_{t} is the robot state, including the base pose and joint configuration, 𝒪 \mathcal{O} is the set of task-relevant objects, and p t k p^{k}_{t} is the pose of object k k . The symbolic state ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} is the set of facts that hold at step t t , such as open ⁡ ( k ) \mathrm{open}(k) , on ⁡ ( k , k ′ ) \mathrm{on}(k,k^{\prime}) , and held ⁡ ( k ) \mathrm{held}(k) . The agent derives and reconstructs these facts from the simulator state. Figure 2: The RoboCoEvo pipeline. Each round proceeds clockwise, starting with rollouts of the current policy π i \pi_{i} . Policy-Guided Agent Evolution (right): the agent identifies failure modes (FMs) from K K sampled failures and writes a detector d m d_{m} for each FM. The detectors localize failure states in all

Recovery program generation. For each FM, its detected preventive and corrective states are partitioned into development and held-out validation sets. The agent develops a shared failure recovery program ρ m \rho_{m} using simulator states restored from the development set. Following a code-as-policy approach, ρ m \rho_{m} is implemented as a finite-state machine over s t s_{t} that composes navigation and manipulation skills with planned motions ( Garrett et al., 2025 ; Sahoo et al., 2026 ) . Recovery success is defined as completion of the subtask at which the original execution failed. The program undergoes iterative refinement and is accepted only when its recovery success rate reaches at least 70 % 70\% on the held-out validation set. The recovery programs evolve alongside the policy. In each subsequent round, the agent develops new programs for newly identified FMs and refines existing programs for FMs that persist. These refinements aim to broaden the range of failure states that the programs can address, improve their recovery success rates, and more precisely target the weaknesses revealed by the current policy.

The accepted recovery program ρ m \rho_{m} is then executed from the detected failure states and from their perturbed copies without further agent intervention. Only successful recoveries are retained, and together they constitute the corrective experience R i R_{i} of round i i . Augmentation thus yields additional corrective experience from a limited number of observed failures, which reduces the number of rollouts required.

original_quotes.quote: We compare the stateless baseline with fourteen adaptation mechanisms, built from four ICL policies and two weight-update rules. ICL replays prior attempts as conversations, including environment observations and outcome feedback. Under a bounded token allowance, two retention policies determine how context is managed: FIFO evicts the oldest episodes to admit new ones, whereas Prefix stops admitting episodes after the first overflow. Two admission policies determine which attempts are eligible: All selects the highest-reward attempt from every round, even if it failed; Successful selects at most one successful attempt per task, from the first round that produces one.

GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) updates a persistent LoRA adapter ( Hu et al., 2022 ) from each round’s attempts: advantages are rewards relative to the round’s mean, and the loss is PPO’s clipped surrogate ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , without a KL penalty or standard-deviation normalization. SDPO ( Hübotter et al., 2026a ) trains a persistent LoRA adapter on the agent’s own attempts by minimizing the reverse KL divergence to a self-teacher’s next-token distributions, with no policy-gradient term. The self-teacher receives the agent’s original context augmented with a successful sibling attempt or, when none is available, the attempt’s feedback. Its weights start as the student’s and then track them as an exponential moving average. Each hybrid combines one ICL policy with one weight-update rule. Each round’s attempts feed both channels: the update trains the adapter on them, conditioned on the context they were generated with, and the ICL policy chooses which of them to keep in the context for later attempts. Appendix A gives the formal interfaces and losses.

Episodes contain actions, environment observations, and final outcome feedback, replayed oldest first between the system prompt and the current task. All admission selects the highest-reward attempt from each round, including failures. Successful admission selects at most one successful attempt per task, from the first round containing a success. It therefore changes both outcome filtering and the number of episodes a task may contribute. FIFO removes oldest whole episodes until the context fits; Prefix permanently stops admitting episodes at the first overflow. Neither uses summarization, retrieval, or an external judge. Reward ties, successful-attempt selection, and SDPO donor selection follow the trainer’s attempt order, which verl rearranges to balance sequence lengths.

original_quotes.quote: The procedure, S4, is pool-growing self-training ( Fig. 1 , detailed in Fig. 2 ). In each round the current champion proposes programs and predicts each four times; those it gets wrong at least once join a pool labelled by the interpreter, and a fresh adapter is trained from the base on the whole pool; each round adds twice as many programs as the last (300, 900 and 2100 in total). [RS25,RS26] The rounds share no parameters; the state that persists is the dataset.

S4 changed what S3’s records pointed at ( Section 4 ), and with it the schedule ( Fig. 2 ). Retraining from the base : generation g g ’s candidate is a fresh LoRA trained from the base on the union of every generation’s frontier, not a continuation of generation g − 1 g-1 ’s adapter; only the data of generation g g is new, proposed and predicted by generation g − 1 g-1 ’s champion. Frontier selection : a program enters when at least one of the champion’s 4 sampled predictions (temperature 1.0) is wrong, so the frontier also holds programs it usually gets right: one predicted right with probability 0.9 per sample enters with probability 0.34. [RS25,RS35] Schedule : 300, 600 and 1200 new programs per generation, two passes over the union, no separate replay, so the generations trained on 300, 900 and 2100 records for 75, 225 and 525 steps. [RS25,RS26] These changes were made together and no ablation separates them. Before any verdict, the examiner’s null replicate (base against base) found no discordant item, the base was served at the configuration under which it answers 12 exam items ( Appendix A ), and the examiner’s build was changed so that it identifies the declared base by the checkpoint’s content. With no default, the plain retry loop is the comparison. The coin runs only in simulated runs that carry a named simulator check; other synthetic runs never count, and simulated and real attempts are never mixed in one test. A pass on simulated evidence is a proposal: a person promotes the candidate, and the record says it was promoted on simulation evidence. A real robot never starts a task with an untested candidate. Demotion needs no test: a default whose real attempt ends in a protective stop or guard trip loses its place at once, and the default it replaced, recorded by the promotion, becomes the default again; with no predecessor the slot is empty and the retry loop runs. Forgetting and erasure. Three states per episode: full, compressed (only the fields consolidation and recall read) and abstracted (for an episode a decided procedure rests on: its deviations from the procedure’s sequence and a reference to it). Integrity is kept by a keyed hash, so deleting the key makes the evidence unverifiable. When an episode is erased, a candidate record is recomputed from the remaining ones; a decided record is corrected from the erased episode’s own outcome and dropped below the minimums, with an audit entry that names the record and the cause, never the person. Erasure always wins over retention.

The measurements are simulations; no real robot and no real users were involved. The memory rules were re-implemented in Python for the benchmarks and follow the specification, not the shipped code. The benchmarks of the tables below, the default-demotion replay and the router follow-ups were planned in writing before they ran, with hypotheses and pass criteria fixed in advance and not changed afterwards. Three measurements had no written plan: the capacity table through the production code, the width-and-shape runs and the vary measurement; numbers marked as found after a first look (the single large matrix on rewordings, the windows of the promotion test) are exploratory. Each store writes its full state, including tombstones and blocked ids, to one JSON file and can restore it; Ledger+Ep writes both stores to the same file.
